**Short answer:** No. These counts don't show suicide prevention growing as an OIG theme. They show a drop, but the drop is probably mostly an artifact of how the data is built.

**Reports with at least one recommendation mentioning "suicide"** (data as of 2026-11-04, not stale):

| Year published | Reports | Matching recommendations | Still open |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 (for context) | 32 | 77 | 2 |
| 2024 | **56** | 98 | 0 |
| 2025 | **11** | 19 | 6 |

The source is the keyword "suicide" in the VA OIG recommendations data, grouped by publication year.

**What the counts can show**
- The number of published OIG reports whose recommendation text contains the word "suicide" fell sharply from 2024 to 2025, from 56 to 11.
- The 2025 recommendations are less likely to be closed. 6 of 19 are open, against 0 of 98 for 2024. That's what you'd expect for newer recommendations, because they haven't had time to close.

**What the counts cannot show**
- **Growth or decline in emphasis.** A fall can mean OIG paid less attention to the topic. It can also mean inspection protocols changed, fewer reports were published, or the problem improved. I can't tell these apart from the counts. I also didn't pull total report volume per year, so these are raw counts, not shares of all reports.
- **Incomplete 2025 data.** Recommendations often appear after a report is published, so 2025 may be undercounted. The 2025 closure figures are also immature.
- **Topic coverage.** A keyword match only finds reports whose recommendation text says "suicide". It misses related wording such as "lethal means", "safety planning", or "mental health risk". It also catches passing mentions, such as a recommendation on a different subject that cites a suicide case.
- **Report counts versus importance.** A report count says nothing about the severity or scale of the findings. One report can have many recommendations. Reports in the Healthcare Facility Inspection program are published in batches, so program scheduling can move the counts.
- **OIG's own tagging.** OIG's "Suicide Prevention" topic label covers only about a quarter of reports, so I didn't use it for this count.

To test the "growing theme" question, I'd compare these counts against total reports and recommendations per year. I'd also split by report type, and check the 2025 data again once it has matured.

**The median VBA recommendation takes 179 days to close.** The middle half of them close between 134 and 312.5 days (the interquartile range).

**What it measures:** the number of days from the report's publication to the date OIG recorded the recommendation as closed. That closure date appears to be when OIG closed it after reviewing evidence. It can come months after VBA actually did the work. So the figure is not the time VBA took to fix the problem, and it says nothing about whether VBA met its own target dates.

**Details on the sample:**
- The data covers 966 recommendations with VBA as an action office. Of these, 923 are closed and 43 are open.
- The median rests on 914 recommendations that have closure dates. About 6% of closed recommendations, mostly from 2013–2016, have no closure date on OIG's site.
- 110 recommendations were closed on the day the report was published, presumably because the fix was made beforehand. Because they count as zero days, they pull the median down.
- 26 of the closed recommendations (2.8%) were closed as not implemented.
- The open VBA recommendations have a median age of 161 days. The oldest is 1,567 days old, and 17 are more than a year old.
- A recommendation that names more than one office counts toward each of them.

Data is as of 2026-11-04 and is current. The source is VA OIG's recommendations data at https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all.

**1. Orlando VA Medical Center, report 14-00689-142 (published 2014-05-06)**
- OIG recommended strengthening processes so medication and supply carts are secured at all times, and monitoring compliance.
- The facility committed to the following:
  - Staff would lock carts before leaving an exam room.
  - Nurse Managers would review the process one-on-one with nursing staff, and an email would go to all nursing and provider staff.
  - Service Chiefs would run extra training for providers and residents.
  - Nurse Managers would run random, unannounced checks of all carts until compliance reached 90% or higher for 3 consecutive months.
- The recommendation is closed-implemented (closed 2014-09-25).

- OIG found that some medication cart drawers weren't secured because of faulty locking mechanisms. It recommended strengthening processes so carts are secured at all times, and monitoring compliance.
- The facility committed to the following:
  - Carts without working locks would be repaired or replaced. Six replacement carts had been received, 26 more were on order, and the remaining carts were still being acquired.
  - In the meantime, carts would stay in a locked medication room unless in use.
  - The Bar Code Medication Administration (BCMA) Coordinator would round on all inpatient areas to check and document compliance.
- The recommendation is closed-implemented (closed 2015-03-11).
- Link: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-atlanta-va-1

- **Open and closed status is only part of the picture.** It shows how recommendations are being handled. It doesn't measure overall quality.
